doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Memorable concerto performances in Germany, Evanston and Prague
summary: Levy recalls performing the concerto with Hohner's accordion orchestra, the Evanston Symphony and the Czech National Symphony in Prague.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Yeah. We are a fan of his show on the radio. But it’s interesting, you said because you wrote the first concerto pre-Finale, that you hadn’t really heard it. But Finale and those things can also affect you like if you have decent playback by the time you’re done you’ve heard this thing hundreds of times. And it’s been my experience – I’m talking mostly about big band charts, that I hear it played by live people and sometimes there’s a moment of disappointment, probably because it’s not perfectly in tune like Finale, right? And then of course you get used to it and it’s better because real people are playing it.

Yeah. Well I mean of course, depending on the quality of the orchestra and of the conductor, there have been, like I said I performed this thing probably 35 times, and certain performances stand out in my mind. It’s like an absolute synergy between me and the conductor and the orchestra, where it’s like thrilling; and other ones were like, kind of like dragging a mule. “Come on guys!” One of the most surprising performances of it that I ever did was Hohner, you know they’re headquartered in Germany in Bavaria in a little town called Trossingen and I’ve worked with Hohner for years now. They have an accordion orchestra and I performed my concerto with the accordion orchestra twice, or

maybe three times. And the third time it was amazing. Because they knew the piece, the conductor was really great, and I knew a lot of these people and it just had a beautiful vibe. It was just – yeah playing, performing and playing with the Evanston Symphony was special too because I live here and the hall was sold out, I knew some of the people in the orchestra. It was a very special feeling. And the conductor is a really good jazz pianist. And we did an encore, it was a Valentine’s Day concert. We did an encore just playing “My Funny Valentine,” me and him. You should look that up. It’s really good. We just like – it was kind of magical. And so yeah, and also I have to say that second movement, it’s kind of an earworm. I’ve always been drawn to melody you know. I can hear and write all kinds of abstract stuff but somehow I’m more deeply committed to something that’s a memorable melody. That to me is like a statement. It’s like a speech. You’re really saying something. You know? So when I played it in Prague I recorded it, the professional recording is with the Czech National Symphony Orchestra, and I recorded it with them in Prague and then we did it in concert at this beautiful concert hall they have called the Rudolfinum, and I just felt like I had written that movement for those people in that city. It just felt like okay, this is where this second movement lives. It’s right here in Prague. And the audience really loved the performance. I had to do two or three solo encores after I did the concerto.
